newsitem.title: USA: Senate threat, and talks, on chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Senate threat, and talks, on chemical treaty.

text.p: Democrats vowed on Wednesday to hold up Senate business to force Republicans to set a date for debate on a treaty banning chemical weapons, but later talks appeared to open the possibility of easing the threat.

The Clinton administration is pushing hard for Senate approval of the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention which outlaws such weapons worldwide, but the treaty remains bottled up in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle issued the gridlock threat at a morning news conference, saying,"I think it's the only leverage we've got."
But on Wednesday evening an aide said that Daschle and Republican Leader Trent Lott had had a "good discussion" that looked "potentially promising," although there were no assurances.

The issue is to be discussed at a Democratic party caucus on Thursday morning. A key question is whether the Senate will be able to go forward with reported compromise legislation expressing congressional concern over the surging movement of drugs from Mexico to the United States.

The administration says the United States must ratify the chemical weapons treaty before it comes into force on April 29 or it will have no voice in implementing it. The treaty bans the production, stockpiling and use of poison gases.
Congress takes a two-week recess starting on Monday, leaving less than three weeks for debate and a vote. A two-thirds Senate majority is needed for approval.

Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, reiterated his strong opposition to the treaty in a Senate speech late on Wednesday, but pledged to work with the administration and others to try to resolve differences.
"But if we are to do so, the administration needs to return to the bargaining table and negotiate with my staff in good faith," he said.
"And they need to realise, in no uncertain terms, that unless they satisfy a number of concerns ... I am not going to move the CWC. Period," Helms said.
Helms called the April 29 deadline "artificial" and a "contrived myth of cataclysmic consequences." He said he would not be "blackmailed" into permitting a flawed treaty to be approved.
He said he continued to want action on other issues, including reform of U.S. foreign affairs agencies and United Nations reform, before turning to the treaty.

Administration officials have been meeting with a group of senators to try to meet some of Helms' objections without dealing a fatal blow to U.S. participation in the pact. Lott said progress had been made and that it was possible the treaty could reach the floor after the recess.
"I am working aggressively to address concerns on all sides of this issue," he said. "We are talking."
He told a reporter: "Of course you have to work with the chairman (Helms)."
